sections.h2: Written notices a Maryland landlord must give
sections.html:
There are four main ones, and each runs on its own clock: a notice of intent to sue for unpaid rent, a breach notice, a notice that ends the tenancy, and a final notice of the eviction date. The reason for the eviction picks the notice. A defective one can lead a court to dismiss the complaint or vacate a warrant.

SituationNotice and length
Unpaid rent (Real Property § 8-401)Written notice of intent to file, 10 days to pay
Lease violation, fixed-term lease (§ 8-402.1)30 days written notice
Violation showing clear and imminent danger (§ 8-402.1)14 days written notice
Ending a month-to-month tenancy or a written lease term over one week (§ 8-402)60 days
Ending a year-to-year tenancy (§ 8-402)90 days (180 for farm tenancies other than tobacco)
Ending a week-to-week tenancy (§ 8-402)7 days with a written lease, 21 days without
Warrant of restitution issued (§ 8-407)At least 6 days before the scheduled eviction

The notice must be on the Judiciary's form, DC-CV-115, and it gives the tenant 10 days to pay before the landlord may file. Section 8-401 allows delivery by certified first-class mail, by posting on the door, or electronically if the tenant chose that method. Electronic notice needs proof of transmission.

The landlord's sworn complaint must state the date the notice was given, and the court may dismiss a complaint for sufficient cause. Only base rent counts toward the 10-day demand. Utilities, maintenance and other charges do not. Late fees are capped too: no more than 5 percent of the late rent, and on a partial payment the fee can apply only to the unpaid portion.

sections.h2: What changes for a lease violation?
sections.html:
The landlord has to wait 30 days after giving written notice that the tenant is in violation and that the landlord wants the property back. Section 8-402.1 covers a fixed-term lease that allows repossession for a breach, and the tenant or person in possession must refuse to comply.

If the breach shows a clear and imminent danger of serious harm to people or property, the wait is cut to 14 days. A tenant ordered out can still appeal to the circuit court within 10 days of the judgment and remain in the home by filing an affidavit, posting a bond, paying back rent and court costs, and covering the landlord's losses from the holdover.

sections.h2: Ending a tenancy without a violation
sections.html:
For most residential tenancies, the landlord gives 60 days. Real Property § 8-402(c) sets 60 days for a month-to-month tenancy or a written lease for a stated term over one week, 90 days for year-to-year, and 7 or 21 days for week-to-week depending on whether there is a written lease.

A few related rules shape the timeline:

  • If the landlord has received a notice of intent to foreclose and wants to end the tenancy, the notice is at least 30 days for month-to-month or week-to-week tenancies and 60 days for year-to-year. The rule does not reach Baltimore City or Montgomery County, landlords with five or more residential units in the state, or a property under a docketing order.
  • Taking rent after notice does not waive the notice or a judgment unless the parties agree otherwise in writing.
  • A tenant who stays past the end of the lease owes at least prorated rent at the lease rate for the holdover period.
  • A rent increase generally takes effect only at renewal and needs 90 days written notice, unless it is part of a notice ending the tenancy.

This notice goes out three ways at once and must carry specific details. Section 8-407 calls for first-class mail with a certificate of mailing, a posting on the front door backed by a date-stamped photo, and email or text if the landlord has the tenant's address or number.

The notice has to include:

  • The court case number, the tenant's name as used in the case and the property address
  • The date the warrant was ordered and the initial eviction date
  • A statement that the eviction can be avoided by returning possession or, where available, by redeeming, with the amount due if redemption is still open
  • A statement that this is the final notice even if the eviction is delayed
  • A warning that belongings may be lost, a list of legal help resources, and the landlord's phone, email and mailing address

A landlord may charge the tenant no more than $5 for giving it. If the landlord hands the sheriff or constable the mailing certificate, a timestamped door photo and a signed affidavit from whoever posted the notice, notice is presumed proper, though a tenant can challenge that. When the sheriff doubts notice was given, the warrant cannot be carried out without a further court order. Local governments may set the notice period anywhere from 4 to 14 days.

Lockouts and utility shutoffs are both banned. Under § 8-216, a landlord can take possession only through a warrant of restitution carried out by a sheriff or constable, or when the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit.

Section 8-208.1 also bars suing for possession, or ending a periodic tenancy, because a tenant made a good-faith complaint, joined a tenants' group, took part in a lawsuit against the landlord, or called police or emergency services. The tenant can raise this as a defense or as a damages claim, with damages up to three months' rent plus fees. Retaliation relief generally requires the tenant to be current on rent, and anything done more than six months after the protected activity cannot be treated as retaliatory. The section has no exception for a landlord who is selling.

sections.h2: When the landlord wants to sell a rented house
sections.html:
For a rental with three or fewer dwelling units, the owner generally must offer the tenant a chance to buy before listing or marketing the home. Real Property § 8-119 gives that right to a named lessee who has lived in the property at least six months.

The owner mails written notice on the form set by the Secretary of Housing and Community Development, by first-class mail with a certificate of mailing or by a tracked delivery service, and sends a copy to the Office of Tenant and Landlord Affairs. The tenant then has 30 days to deliver a written offer. If the offer matches the notice terms, the owner has 5 days to accept. A violation can bring a fine of up to $1,000.

The section does not cover several kinds of transfers, including:

  • Sales to a family member or to a business the owner wholly owns
  • Transfers by foreclosure, tax sale, court order or bankruptcy
  • Transfers by an estate, guardianship or trust fiduciary, or by will or inheritance

A landlord may enter to show the home to buyers on 24 hours written notice, generally Monday through Saturday between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. Properties with four or more units fall outside the right of first refusal.

faqs.q: How many days notice before a landlord files for unpaid rent?
faqs.a: Ten days. The landlord uses the Judiciary's form DC-CV-115, states the rent due, and gives the tenant 10 days to pay before filing in District Court.

faqs.q: How long is a notice to end a month-to-month tenancy?
faqs.a: Sixty days in writing from the landlord. The tenant generally gives 30 days, unless the lease requires more.

faqs.q: Can a landlord evict on 14 days notice?
faqs.a: Only for a lease violation that shows a clear and imminent danger of serious harm to people or property. Other breach notices run 30 days.

faqs.q: Is notice required before the sheriff arrives?
faqs.a: Yes. After a warrant of restitution, the landlord must send written notice at least 6 days before the scheduled eviction by mail, posting and electronic message when contact details are known. Some local governments set 4 to 14 days.

faqs.q: Does a tenant get first chance to buy a rented house?
faqs.a: Often. A named tenant of at least six months in a property with three or fewer units has a right of first refusal, with exceptions for family transfers, foreclosure, estate transfers and a few others.
